title: A clinical instrument that reads an individual’s psychiatric state

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a clinical instrument that repeatedly estimates a specified psychiatric state in an individual: how that person’s illness is changing now, rather than simply whether they resemble a diagnostic group or have an elevated lifetime risk. The intended capability is reliable longitudinal measurement that can be used repeatedly in ordinary care. This is a proposed enabling technology; the supplied evidence does not establish that a broadly applicable psychiatric state meter exists.

The state being estimated would need an explicit definition and a defensible connection to the measured signals. A biological recording, reproducible speech measure or continuous behavioral measurement would not become a state meter merely by producing a numerical score. Its developers would need to show that the score tracks clinically meaningful changes in the intended psychological state. The supplied review emphasizes well-articulated causal models linking brain activity to psychological phenomena; an articulated model is a basis for validation, not proof that the signal causes the illness.

Conceptual distinction: predicting relapse and measuring current state are different capabilities. A stable vulnerability marker could predict future relapse while remaining unchanged as a person becomes ill or recovers. PSY-06 therefore requires evidence of sensitivity to within-person change as well as useful prediction. It also remains distinct from PSY-01: assigning a mechanism-defined disease category addresses what disease a person has, whereas a state meter addresses its changing condition, even if both systems use the same sensors.

significance.text: Psychiatric assessment relies substantially on symptoms, interviews and clinical history. The supplied sources describe measurement limitations and efforts to measure symptoms and behavior more rigorously, but they do not justify declaring existing assessments generally inadequate for trials, treatment titration or clinical care. A validated state instrument would add a repeatable measurement capability whose value could be tested against these existing assessments.

Conditional significance: the direct advance would be an individual longitudinal measurement system with demonstrated state validity and prospective predictive value. Reliable estimates between clinical visits could make changes more observable, and repeated measurements could give trials a better-characterized way to follow illness trajectories. The revolutionary element would be the ability to measure a specified changing state with known performance, rather than infer it only from occasional assessments.

Conditional downstream possibilities include earlier warning of relapse, more informative treatment monitoring and better-supported decisions about treatment selection or adjustment. These benefits would require additional demonstrations: predicting deterioration does not establish that acting on the prediction prevents it, and detecting change does not establish which treatment will help. The instrument would provide measurement; discovery of disease causes and effective treatments would remain separate achievements.

Limit on the laboratory-test analogy: the proposal does not imply one universal number for mental illness, a direct reading of subjective experience or replacement of clinical judgment. Its strongest defensible form is a measure of a specified state in a specified context. Performance for one disorder, population or treatment setting would not establish equivalent performance elsewhere.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an individual-level measure that combines known reliability, a clearly defined psychiatric target, a defensible model connecting the signal to that target and prospective clinical validity. Group-level biological differences are insufficient: an average difference between patients and controls does not establish a test that can identify an individual’s condition or guide that person’s treatment.

A concrete psychometric barrier arises when measures developed for experimental contrasts are repurposed for individual assessment. Protocols can emphasize within-person contrasts while minimizing between-person variation, making them poorly suited to distinguishing individuals. The problem is not that a signal necessarily loses reliability when it enters a clinic; it is that its original design and validation may not support the clinical inference being demanded. The supplied review also identifies poor internal and test-retest reliability in many candidate biomarkers, particularly where patient data are more variable.

Further barriers include inconsistent replication, incomplete theory and unclear links between physiological measurements and psychological processes. A reproducible biological association can still be non-specific to the state of interest. Developers must establish what a measurement means, which competing explanations remain possible and whether its interpretation holds in the intended clinical population.

Engineering and validation synthesis: a useful state meter must be stable when the target state is stable yet responsive when that state changes. This requires distinguishing clinically meaningful change from measurement noise and specifying how repeat measurements are collected and interpreted in routine care. Neither a reliable ranking of people nor a successful outcome predictor alone resolves this longitudinal measurement problem.

current_state.text: Peter E. Clayson’s December 2025 review, “Translating neurophysiological biomarkers into clinical tools,” reports stalled clinical translation, inconsistent replication and reliability problems. Its focus is event-related potentials, illustrated with error-related negativity, rather than an exhaustive survey of every psychiatric measurement technology. The supplied review record contains its abstract, not its full text. That abstract supports the stated psychometric barriers and a roadmap connecting psychometric work with analytic validation, clinical validation and qualification for a context of use.

David Adam’s October 28, 2026 Nature news feature presents personalized psychiatry as a future vision and describes continuing obstacles to routine clinical translation. It discusses efforts involving reproducible speech measurements and continuous digital phenotyping, alongside the difficulty of converting biological group differences into useful individual tests. These are research directions discussed in a news feature, not demonstrations in the supplied evidence of a clinically validated, broadly applicable state meter.

The retained Nature text includes Kenneth Kendler’s assessment that investigated hormone and metabolite measures have generally lacked specificity. This observation concerns those classes of measures and should not be generalized to every psychiatric biomarker. Although the reconciled research reported that the passage could not be relocated during an earlier check, the supplied validated review confirms its presence in the retained text. The article record is partial and affected by an access gate, so the available passages do not establish complete article coverage.

A 2025 study by Mollon and colleagues found limited stability and specificity in the psychiatric polygenic risk scores it tested, including scores for schizophrenia, depression and alcohol-use disorder in White British UK Biobank participants. The authors concluded that these limitations restricted the scores’ clinical utility. This supports a bounded conclusion about the tested scores and population, rather than universal failure of every psychiatric polygenic-score application. The supplied assessment used the abstract; full methods and figure images were not inspected. Genetic risk prediction also addresses a different target from measurement of a changing psychiatric state.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material documents substantial translational gaps but does not establish the absence of every clinically useful psychiatric biomarker or every diagnostic biomarker standard in DSM practice. Its dated coverage consists of the 2025 review and polygenic-score study and the October 28, 2026 feature. No bounded freshness-search record was supplied, so this record cannot claim exhaustive coverage through November 1, 2026. Those limitations leave the broader landscape uncertain; they do not show that a particular unassessed result is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: define the psychiatric state, intended population, clinical setting and decision context before testing. Lock and preregister the measurement procedure and prediction model, then prospectively test whether the instrument improves prediction of relapse or treatment response over a prespecified clinical-rating benchmark in an external sample. These design requirements are proposed for this concept; they are not established standards prescribed by the supplied sources.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed convincing demonstration

completion_criteria.text: The validation foundation should include analytic validity, clinical validity and an explicit context of use. Clayson’s review supports organizing biomarker development around these elements and rigorous psychometric assessment. The instrument’s reliability must be characterized for its intended use, rather than inferred from an experimental group effect or borrowed from a different population.
completion_criteria.label: The validation foundation should include analytic validity, clinical

completion_criteria.text: Proposed state-tracking demonstration: show test-retest reliability under stable conditions and sensitivity to clinically meaningful within-person change across repeated assessments. The study should explicitly distinguish changing state information from stable risk information. Better relapse prediction alone would establish predictive value, while a classifier separating cases from controls in a convenience sample would establish neither the required longitudinal capability nor routine-care usefulness.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed state-tracking demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce the result with independent investigators or sites and demonstrate repeated use under the collection conditions expected in ordinary care. Report measurement uncertainty, failure conditions and the populations and settings actually tested. No numerical acceptance threshold is established by the supplied material; thresholds should be justified for the intended use before evaluation. Finite successful studies would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical-utility extension: if the instrument is claimed to improve treatment decisions, prevent relapse or improve patient outcomes, test those benefits separately by evaluating care guided by its measurements. Demonstrating state measurement would complete the central measurement capability within its validated scope; demonstrating better care would support the additional clinical claims.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed clinical-utility extension

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — PSY-01, “Mechanism-defined diseases in place of the major syndromes”: both concepts could use biological or behavioral measurements, but their outputs differ. PSY-01 concerns disease identity and classification by mechanism; PSY-06 concerns a person’s changing psychiatric state. A successful state instrument would not by itself establish a new disease taxonomy.

Roster-based synthesis — PSY-02, “A treatment that changes the course of schizophrenia,” and PSY-03, “Ending the relapsing course of severe mood disorders”: a state instrument could help characterize illness trajectories and evaluate treatment effects. Measuring improvement or predicting relapse would not establish that a treatment changes schizophrenia’s course or ends severe mood-disorder recurrence. Each remains a separate therapeutic achievement.

Roster-based synthesis — PSY-04, “Primary prevention that lowers incidence of a major disorder,” and PSY-11, “Prevention of post-traumatic stress disorder by blocking consolidation”: PSY-06 could provide measurements useful to prevention studies, but detecting a changing state or elevated risk does not demonstrate reduced incidence. PSY-11 additionally specifies a preventive intervention on memory consolidation, which is distinct from measuring its effects.

Roster-based synthesis — PSY-05, “Medicines designed from a confirmed human disease mechanism,” and PSY-07, “Reliable causal control of a core symptom by a defined circuit”: a state measure might help evaluate drug effects or responses to circuit interventions. Its validity would not establish a confirmed disease mechanism, rationally designed medicine or causal control of a symptom. Conversely, controlling a symptom would not establish a broadly useful state instrument.

Roster-based synthesis — PSY-08, “Selective and durable modification of a pathological memory,” PSY-09, “A time-limited reset of severe addiction,” and PSY-10, “Reopening plasticity that can repair an established psychiatric deficit”: these concern interventions that alter memory, addiction or an established deficit. PSY-06 could potentially measure relevant changes, but measurement success would establish none of those intervention-specific effects or their durability.

Roster-based synthesis — PSY-12, “A session-level amplifier that lets brief psychotherapy match a full course”: repeated state measurements could help study when and how psychotherapy produces change. Demonstrating that an abbreviated course matches a full course would still require direct comparative treatment evidence. PSY-06 supplies a possible measurement capability, while PSY-12 specifies a therapeutic performance outcome.

change_log.change: Preserved PSY-06’s identity while defining the target as a specified, changing psychiatric state.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports a coherent measurement goal without establishing an achieved or universally applicable state meter.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical criticism of interviews and rating scales with a bounded account of measurement limitations.
change_log.reason: The supplied sources do not establish that existing assessments are generally inadequate for trials, titration or care.

change_log.change: Corrected the reliability explanation and distinguished an articulated causal model from demonstrated causation.
change_log.reason: Experimental protocols can be poorly suited to individual differences; clinical use does not inherently cause reliability loss, and model articulation alone does not prove causality.

change_log.change: Added sensitivity to within-person change and explicit separation of state tracking from stable risk prediction.
change_log.reason: Outcome prediction and repeatability alone do not demonstrate measurement of a changing state.

change_log.change: Scoped the December 2025 review to event-related potentials and preserved its abstract-only access limitation.
change_log.reason: Its findings should not be presented as a full-text, exhaustive assessment of psychiatric biomarkers.

change_log.change: Corrected the reported availability of Kendler’s observation and limited it to hormone and metabolite measures.
change_log.reason: The validated review confirms the passage in the retained Nature text; its scope does not justify a universal non-specificity claim.

change_log.change: Restricted the polygenic-score conclusion to the tested scores and population and removed the categorical DSM biomarker-absence claim.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not support either unrestricted assertion.

change_log.change: Separated the direct measurement advance from conditional treatment and patient-outcome benefits.
change_log.reason: Predictive or measurement validity does not automatically establish clinical utility.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed validation boundaries and explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Completion requires reproducible performance within a defined use, while related therapeutic and classification innovations remain distinct.

unresolved_issues: The target psychiatric state, instrument modality, intended population and context of use remain unspecified.
The supplied evidence does not identify a candidate instrument that meets the full proposed combination of reliability, sensitivity to change and external prospective validity.
The full Clayson review and the polygenic-score study’s full methods and figures were not available within the supplied assessment; the retained Nature article is partial and access-gated.
No bounded freshness-search record establishes exhaustive coverage through November 1, 2026.
The retained Nature text resolves the passage’s availability in this evidence record but cannot determine what was available during the earlier checking session.
Appropriate performance thresholds and the clinical value of acting on state measurements remain to be established for a specified use.
